## Cybersecurity

- `creeper-virus` [cyber] — Say: Creeper (1971), considered the first computer worm/virus, did no damage – it only displayed "I'm the creeper, catch me if you can!". | Don't say: that it spread worldwide. | Visual: retro CRT with the message.
- `reaper` [cyber] — Say: Soon after Creeper, a program called Reaper was written to chase it and delete it – often called the first antivirus. | Don't say: exact date. | Visual: two pixel creatures – one fleeing, one chasing – across a network map.
- `elk-cloner` [cyber] — Say: Elk Cloner (1982), one of the first viruses to spread "in the wild", was written by a 15-year-old as a prank on the Apple II – it showed a short poem. | Don't say: invented lines of the poem (safe to quote only: "Elk Cloner: The program with a personality"). | Visual: floppy disk + Apple II-style screen with "Elk Cloner: The program with a personality".
- `brain-virus` [cyber] — Say: Brain (1986), considered the first PC virus, was written by two brothers in Pakistan – who put their real names, address and phone number inside it. | Don't say: that they were arrested. | Visual: floppy disk + hex dump with a phone icon.
- `aids-trojan-ransomware` [cyber] — Say: The first known ransomware, the "AIDS Trojan" (1989), was mailed to victims on floppy disks and demanded payment sent by post. | Don't say: exact ransom amount. | Visual: envelope with a floppy disk and a padlock on files, "1989".
- `morris-worm` [cyber] — Say: The Morris worm (1988), one of the first internet worms, spread so fast that it slowed down a large part of the internet of that time; its author was the first person convicted under the US computer-fraud law. | Don't say: exact numbers of computers. | Visual: network map lighting up node by node.
- `iloveyou` [cyber] — Say: In 2000 the "ILOVEYOU" virus spread worldwide through an email with the subject "ILOVEYOU" and an attachment called LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU. | Don't say: damage figures. | Visual: email inbox with a heart subject line and a suspicious `.TXT.vbs` attachment.
- `wannacry-killswitch` [cyber] — Say: The WannaCry ransomware (2017) was slowed down when a security researcher registered a strange web domain he found in its code – a hidden "kill switch". | Don't say: that he "stopped it completely". | Visual: big red switch labelled `kill switch` next to a long gibberish domain name.
- `stuxnet` [cyber] — Say: Stuxnet is known as the first cyber weapon to cause physical damage – it sabotaged uranium-enrichment centrifuges. | Don't say: who built it. | Visual: spinning centrifuge outlines with one wobbling, code overlay.
- `enigma-turing` [cyber] — Say: During WWII, Alan Turing and the team at Bletchley Park helped break the German Enigma cipher. | Don't say: exact number of lives saved or "ended the war". | Visual: Enigma rotors and keyboard lamps.
- `caesar-cipher` [cyber] — Say: Julius Caesar encrypted messages by shifting each letter 3 places in the alphabet – one of the oldest known ciphers. | Don't say: that it is secure today. | Visual: two alphabet rings offset by 3 (A→D, B→E), "HELLO → KHOOR".
- `phishing-ph` [cyber] — Say: "Phishing" is spelled with "ph" as a nod to "phreaking" – the hacking of telephone networks by early hackers. | Don't say: a specific year of the first phishing attack. | Visual: phone handset turning into a fishing hook catching an email.
